stories.headline: Polling Firm Admits Its Results Were Fabricated; FCC Chair Warns Broadcasters Over 'Fake Polls'
stories.summary:
Wedgewood Polling, a national polling organization whose results were cited by several news outlets, said Tuesday that the vast majority of its data had been fabricated. It described the operation as an "experimental project to demonstrate the vulnerabilities" of the political polling industry. The statement came after the polling analysis site FiftyPlusOne questioned the veracity of its results.

Wedgewood's data had been included in the databases of FiftyPlusOne and The New York Times, which have since removed it. MS NOW, Newsweek, Decision Desk HQ and Mediaite had also cited its polls. Wedgewood called itself a "fictional entity run by a small group of industry veterans" and said the episode showed "a systemic breakdown in media vetting and data aggregation." FiftyPlusOne and the Times rejected the claim that they aggregated the data without checking, saying they had contacted the firm with questions about its methods before including it. Columbia University statistician Andrew Gelman said it was "kind of suspicious" that the firm described it as an experiment only on the day it was caught.

On Wednesday, Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr said on X that broadcasters could violate their regulatory obligations by airing "fake polls," advising them to avoid "News Distortions" or "Broadcast Hoaxes." Without citing evidence or specific polls, he said there had been a "significant surge in entirely Fake Polls and Suppression Polls" this election season.

The disclosure bears on races including the Michigan Senate primary and comes two weeks before the midterms, when polling shapes campaign strategy and media narratives. Right-leaning outlets have highlighted it as a failure of media scrutiny, while others note the data was caught by the polling-analysis community itself.

stories.headline: White House Gives Politico 48 Hours to Retract Stories or Face 'Consequences'
stories.summary:
The White House counsel's office warned Politico in a Monday letter that it had 48 hours to retract or correct recent stories about alleged White House staff drama, or face unspecified consequences. The deadline expires Thursday, according to Axios.

The demand threatens to escalate already tense relations between the administration and Politico, and more broadly the press corps covering President Trump. Politico, CNN and MS NOW are already banned from covering Trump in the Oval Office.

Separately, White House Correspondents' Association President Jacqui Heinrich on Wednesday condemned the White House's decision to restrict access for Andrew Feinberg, a correspondent for The Independent. Feinberg was scheduled to serve as the print pool reporter when Trump lashed out at him in the Oval Office earlier this week. Press freedom advocates see the moves as pressure on coverage, while the administration has previously argued that some reporting is inaccurate. The White House had not publicly detailed what consequences it might impose.

stories.headline: AI Models Increasingly Capable of Planning Attacks on Power and Water Systems, Research Finds
stories.summary:
The most advanced AI models are now capable of blueprinting cyberattacks on critical services such as power grids and water systems with alarming success rates, according to new research from the cybersecurity company Frenos. The findings were reported by Axios.

Researchers found that top-tier frontier models are dangerously adept at mapping out attacks on infrastructure. The report warns that critical infrastructure operators are running out of time to prepare, and that it is only a matter of time before freely available AI models make such hacks easier to execute.

The research arrives amid wider concern about AI security. The creators of PHP, which powers as much as 70 percent of websites, said Wednesday that AI was used to pinpoint two vulnerabilities in the language that hackers could exploit. Congressional leaders are also weighing regulatory action and public safety checks on advanced AI companies. The findings add pressure on utilities and regulators to strengthen defenses for systems that serve millions of people.

stories.headline: Mexico Charges Former Chihuahua Prosecutor With Treason Over US Agents' Role in Drug Lab Raid
stories.summary:
Mexican federal prosecutors have charged Cesar Jauregui Moreno, who served as attorney general of Chihuahua state from 2023 to this year, with treason. They allege he allowed US agents to take part in an April raid on a suspected drug lab without proper authorization. Federal Attorney General Ernestina Godoy Ramos said he permitted foreign agents to carry out activities reserved for Mexican authorities and failed to share information. Jauregui, a member of the conservative opposition PAN party, was arrested over the weekend and denies the allegations.

The operation came to light after a convoy returning from raids on suspected methamphetamine labs plunged into a ravine on April 19. Two US agents, reportedly working for the CIA, and two Mexican state investigators were killed. At the time Jauregui described the Americans as embassy "instructor officers" doing training work. A court hearing is set for Saturday, and a judge must decide whether there is enough evidence to proceed. He also faces state charges, including abuse of public office, and denied at a Sunday hearing that he instructed or consented to US involvement.

The case touches a sensitive issue between the two countries. President Claudia Sheinbaum has faced pressure from President Trump to crack down on drug trafficking but has repeatedly declined offers of US-led operations, insisting foreign officials may operate in Mexico only with prior federal clearance. Supporters of the prosecution see it as defending sovereignty, while the defendant's party aligns him with the political opposition.

stories.headline: New Mexico Judge Orders Meta to Pay $25 Billion Over Misleading User Data Claims
stories.summary:
A New Mexico judge on Wednesday ordered Meta Platforms, the parent of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, to pay $25 billion after finding the company spent years misleading the public about how it handled Facebook user data. The ruling followed a two-week trial earlier this year and is the largest fine ever imposed on the company. Judge Francis Mathew wrote that the violations were "willful" and spanned more than 11 years, from 2010 to 2021.

The case grew out of the Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which a political consulting firm used Facebook user information, including in work tied to the 2016 presidential election. New Mexico's lawyers sued over statements by Meta executives that user data was never sold or shared with third parties, when it had been. The judge said communications among senior executives, including Mark Zuckerberg, were "designed to mislead the public," and that the lies went "to the heart of Facebook's core business practices."

The full penalty, based on thousands of violations of state law, was calculated at $219 billion, but the judge reduced it to $25 billion, an amount roughly equal to Meta's quarterly profits. The company has faced other large penalties this year, including an $18 billion deal with California over child safety and a fine of nearly $1 billion in a separate New Mexico case over the safety of its platforms for children. A Meta spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and the company is widely expected to appeal.

stories.headline: Armed Federal Agents Knock on Doors Seeking Noncitizen Voters Ahead of Midterms
stories.summary:
Armed, uniformed Department of Homeland Security agents have been visiting homes in several states to ask residents about their immigration status and whether they have registered or voted, a CBS News investigation found. The visits, carried out by Homeland Security Investigations, ramped up in September and continued over the past weekend. On Monday the Justice Department announced that agents in California had arrested more than 20 green card holders accused of illegally registering or voting, including a 72-year-old man from Belize taken from his home in his pajamas.

DHS has alleged that as many as 250,000 noncitizens could be illegally registered to vote, though election experts dispute that figure. The Justice Department says 156 people have been charged with voting-fraud offenses since the start of the Trump administration, out of 227 million registered voters. A DHS spokesperson said the agency is "committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens and only American citizens are electing American leaders."

Critics say the tactic could intimidate lawful voters. Jessica Marsden of Protect Democracy, a left-leaning advocacy group suing over the door-knocking, said it appears "maximally designed to scare lawful voters." Eric Balliet, a former HSI agent with 23 years of service, said he never knew of agents being sent to private homes to verify voter eligibility. Supporters of the effort argue that enforcing citizenship requirements protects election integrity. The Nov. 3 midterms are less than two weeks away, and the lawsuit over the program is pending.

stories.headline: Israeli Fighter Jets Fly Massive Sortie to Iranian Border Days Before Israeli Election
stories.summary:
Dozens of Israeli Air Force fighter jets flew a sortie on Monday that reached the Iranian border, more than 800 miles from Israel, according to Israeli and U.S. officials cited by Axios. The operation was described as a show of "power projection." It took place about a week before Israel's Oct. 27 election and on the same day Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Ovda Air Base.

Officials said the sortie was not connected to Hegseth's visit. Some Israeli and U.S. officials said such exercises are not unusual, while the scale and distance drew attention amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran. Tehran has said it has "unfinished jobs" and has warned Washington against renewed attack.

Separately, congressional candidate Brad Lander said he was detained by the Israel Defense Forces in the West Bank while harvesting olives with Rabbis for Peace volunteers. He told NBC News he was released with a warning while dozens in the group remained in custody, amid growing criticism of settler violence. The Israeli election and the war with Iran remain central to regional tensions.

stories.headline: Trump Invokes Willie Horton Case in North Carolina Senate Rally Against Roy Cooper
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump campaigned in North Carolina on Tuesday for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, attacking former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic nominee, over his criminal justice record. Trump invoked the 1988 Willie Horton case, comparing Cooper to Michael Dukakis, whose presidential campaign was damaged over a Massachusetts prison furlough program.

Trump claimed Cooper "let out hundreds of some of the worst criminals, but 83 or 85, and they killed within a short period of time, 25 people." He argued the allegations against Cooper were more serious than the controversy that hurt Dukakis. The remarks were made at a rally in a key battleground, and Cooper's campaign has not been quoted in the available coverage.

The race is closely watched because control of the Senate is at stake in the Nov. 3 midterms. Early voting is under way, with more than 12 million votes already cast nationwide. Republicans view crime as a central line of attack, while Democrats have focused on the economy and on Trump's low approval ratings. Former President Obama is also set to campaign for Democrats in Georgia next week.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Refuses to Let Trump Administration Restrict Medical Care for Transgender Federal Inmates
stories.summary:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday rejected an emergency request from the Trump administration to enforce a Bureau of Prisons policy that would end hormone treatments and certain surgeries for transgender inmates. In an unsigned order, the justices declined to lift a lower court's block on the policy, leaving it in place while litigation continues. Reports described the vote as 7-2, with two conservative justices dissenting.

The Bureau of Prisons policy would have tapered treatment for inmates currently receiving it and stopped providing gender-affirming procedures going forward. The Justice Department argued that it should be allowed to enforce the new rules immediately. The ruling is a loss for the administration on the Court's emergency docket, where it has frequently prevailed.

The decision is procedural and does not settle the underlying legal questions, which will continue to be argued in the lower courts. Supporters of the policy say it reflects the administration's authority to set prison health standards and to limit taxpayer-funded gender transition care. Civil liberties and medical groups argue that denying established treatment to inmates violates constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.

The ruling arrived as Justice Elena Kagan, speaking Tuesday, criticized recent conservative-majority decisions on redistricting and campaign finance as weakening American democracy, two weeks before the midterm elections. The administration is expected to continue defending the policy as the case proceeds.

stories.headline: Update: Putin Agrees in Principle to Resume Trilateral Ukraine Talks After Witkoff Meeting; Russia Frees American Teacher
stories.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin told U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday that he agrees in principle to resume trilateral peace talks among Russia, Ukraine and the United States, the Kremlin said. Putin's foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said the talks could restart after November 10. Jared Kushner joined the meeting virtually.

Separately, Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher from Michigan jailed for more than four years on accusations that he fought alongside Ukrainian forces, which his family has denied. President Trump praised the release and said the United States was not required to give anything in return. Critics noted that it came after Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russian diesel sales, and one outlet observed that the only concession Putin appears to have made is agreeing to negotiate. Witkoff drew criticism, including from Republican Sen. John Cornyn, after calling Putin a humanitarian.

The meeting followed Oslo talks between Witkoff, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European officials, intended to ease tensions between Kyiv and Washington. In a Fox News interview Wednesday, Zelensky said he would accept freezing the front line to end the war, saying that is a realistic path. Ukraine and its allies say it is now up to Russia to respond to the proposals agreed in Oslo.

The Kremlin also said China has begun preparing for a possible first three-way summit of the Russian, U.S. and Chinese leaders next month. Supporters of the administration's approach say direct engagement is needed to end the war, while critics say it rewards Moscow without securing concessions.

stories.headline: Toledo Chemical Tank Explosion Forces Evacuations Amid Fears of Another Blast
stories.summary:
A chemical tank exploded in Toledo, Ohio, around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday, prompting officials to order everyone within a one-mile radius to evacuate and issue a shelter-in-place order for residents within three miles. More than 900 people live in the evacuation zone, and Mayor Wade Kapszukiewicz said they were believed to have left by Wednesday morning. A sheriff's deputy was injured responding and drove himself to a hospital.

The tank, operated by MC Tank Transport, contained glycidyl methacrylate, an industrial chemical used in plastics, paints and coatings. It is liquid in the tank but becomes a gas when released, and the tank can hold 5,500 gallons. The mayor warned that it could remain explosive for up to 12 hours after the incident, and responders are staying away from the tank because of the risk of further explosions.

Health officials said the chemical is highly toxic on contact or ingestion and can cause burning of the eyes, nose, mouth and skin, as well as headaches, dizziness, nausea and vomiting. Health Department director Karim Baroudi advised residents to close windows and shower if they feel irritation, while crews work to measure air toxicity. Fog hindered drone monitoring early Wednesday. The cause of the explosion is unknown, and officials said conditions would be reassessed later in the day.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Missile Strike on Yemeni Training Camp Kills 73 Security Recruits
stories.summary:
A Houthi ballistic missile strike on a security training camp in Yemen's central Shabwa province has killed 73 people, local authorities said Tuesday, making it the deadliest reported attack since the current escalation began. The Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group fired three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city on Monday. The site, the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, was being used to train recruits for the internal security forces and police.

Shabwa's media office initially reported 53 dead and 200 wounded, but said in a new statement that an investigative committee had raised the death toll to 73, with another 14 people missing. Hospitals were overwhelmed, and the most seriously wounded were moved to Hadramout and Aden, according to deputy governor Fahad al-Khalifi. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani called the attack a war crime, arguing the facility was not a military target. Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Presidential Leadership Council, condemned a "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response."

The Houthis' military spokesman said the group had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations." Yemen's civil war has flared in recent months. Pro-government forces launched a major offensive at the start of October, backed by Saudi-led coalition air support, and retook Red Sea coastal territory overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait that the Houthis seized in September. Heavy fighting continues there, around besieged Taiz, and in Marib and al-Jawf provinces, while the Houthis have fired missiles and drones at Saudi airports, energy facilities and military bases.

stories.headline: Pope Leo Returns to St. Peter's Square for First Audience Since Cancer Surgery
stories.summary:
Pope Leo returned to St. Peter's Square on Wednesday, waving to pilgrims and blessing babies from an open-air popemobile as he held his first general audience since lung cancer surgery eight days ago. The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on October 13 and has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. It was his first audience since October 7.

Leo opened the 50-minute event by thanking the crowd for "the support and prayers," without directly mentioning his health, and spoke in a clear voice. He delivered a sermon in Italian and, in the only notable change from past audiences, offered brief greetings in seven languages rather than nine. Crowds gathered hours ahead in drizzling weather.

Doctors have said the surgery was completed without complications, but they have not disclosed the tumor's size or whether the disease spread to nearby lymph nodes, both key to prognosis. The Vatican has given no schedule beyond Wednesday. The pope is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, and it remains unclear whether the trip will proceed as planned. His lead surgeon has said he could be fully recovered in time, while the Vatican's secretary of state has suggested the pace of his schedule may need to be adjusted. Leo, elected in May 2025, leads the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.

stories.headline: Update: Trump and Zelensky at Odds Despite Oslo Talks as Rift Deepens
stories.summary:
A BBC analysis finds that the relationship between President Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has reached one of its lowest points, even as US envoy Steve Witkoff embraced Zelensky before talks in Oslo. Zelensky posted video of the moment with the message "Ukraine is working for peace," but analysts doubt it dispels his misgivings about US policy.

Trump told Newsmax last week that "Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," and on Monday said "Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about" when asked about the Ukrainian leader's claim that a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history. Zelensky, usually circumspect, told a US congressional delegation of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced fear that a political decision had been made to slow support. On Telegram Monday he wrote that Kyiv has welcomed "literally EVERY attempt" to end the war with dignity, rebutting Trump's charge that he is the main obstacle to a settlement.

The article notes earlier ruptures, including the February 2025 Oval Office clash that led to a week-long suspension of aid, were followed by reversals, and that Trump has swung sharply on other leaders such as Israel's Netanyahu. Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform said Trump can always U-turn but that "this does look bad." Supply of US-made Patriot air defence missiles has slowed to a trickle after this year's US war with Iran and a global shortage.

stories.headline: Update: France Divided Over Who Is to Blame for Riots as Parliamentary Inquiry Proposed
stories.summary:
France remains split over who orchestrated the October 17 riots and what lessons to draw. National Assembly president Yael Braun-Pivet has proposed a parliamentary inquiry into the riots and how they were organised. Reports say more than 3,000 shops and businesses were looted, much of it apparently opportunistic, with some looters trying to sell stolen goods online.

French intelligence had told government circles that left-wing anarchist groups were involved in student protests, and a circled capital A was spray-painted on buildings nationwide. Le Figaro published a September 29 intelligence report alleging student unions and radical-left movements manipulated demonstrations, and suggesting the party La France Insoumise was relying on violence as an electoral strategy ahead of the 2027 presidential election. LFI denies this.

President Emmanuel Macron, viewed by many as a lame duck, and his government are accused of failing to keep the country safe. Macron insists all those responsible for violence or theft will be brought to justice, and online sales platforms say they will help authorities track looters. Police are examining CCTV and social media footage. Some Parisians told the BBC the violence does not represent France and rejected talk of civil war.

stories.headline: Update: Fox News Investigation Finds 101 Groups Across 13 Countries Behind New Rounds of French Protests
stories.summary:
Two days after an estimated 500,000 demonstrators poured into streets across France and clashes left parts of Paris and other cities burning, activists are calling supporters back out on Saturday, Oct. 24, for a second protest billed as "Acte II." A digital map of the plans lists 212 "mobilizations." A separate call has gone out for a coordinated European youth strike on Friday, Nov. 20.

A Fox News Digital investigation says it has identified 101 organizations in 13 countries, including the United States, that are coordinating, organizing or amplifying the protests, up from 54 identified on Monday. According to the report, most of the groups are adult-led, and 33 are led by students or youth. Fox describes the network as a "red-green" alliance of Islamist organizations and far-left, communist and socialist groups, and says some groups use the "Antifa" label. It also cites U.S. academic Hatem Bazian, founder of Students for Justice in Palestine and American Muslims for Palestine, for sharing videos of the protests. Bazian did not respond to a request for comment.

The findings reflect the right-leaning framing of the unrest, which stresses organized, ideologically driven coordination. French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the unrest is being exploited, and he has acknowledged intelligence failures. Critics on the left and many protesters present the demonstrations as a response to broader grievances, including conditions in French schools and wider social frustrations, rather than as a centrally directed campaign. The Fox report's characterization of the groups has not been independently verified in the material provided.

The next test comes Saturday, when authorities must decide how to handle the planned Acte II events. Several French cities have already extended curfews, and about 1,800 people were arrested in earlier violence.

stories.headline: Update: Musk Ordered Starshield Slowdown That Hampered Ukraine, Wall Street Journal Reports
stories.summary:
Elon Musk ordered a slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Starlink satellite internet, according to a Wall Street Journal report citing U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter. Ukraine has said the disruption hampered its ability to respond to Russian attacks. The slowdown reportedly affected Ukrainian drones, airplanes and helicopters.

CBS News, citing its own sources, reported that a decision by Musk led to restrictions on Ukraine's use of SpaceX's satellite communications network, and that he chose to limit access in ways that affected drone operations. The reports come as Musk and President Donald Trump have both recently criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has also flagged disruptions in U.S. intelligence sharing.

The revelation is notable because Starlink and Starshield have been central to Ukrainian battlefield communications, and a single executive's decision can affect military operations. It also arrives amid other Musk-related business news. He said on SpaceX's earnings call that special committees of independent directors at SpaceX and Tesla are examining a possible merger, which he called a good idea. SpaceX reported third-quarter net income of $4.4 billion, well above the average analyst estimate.

It was not clear from the available reporting whether Musk or SpaceX has responded publicly to the specific allegations. The matter is likely to draw scrutiny from lawmakers and Ukrainian officials over reliance on privately controlled infrastructure in wartime.

stories.headline: Trump and Vance Announce $25 Million Fraud Whistleblower Program
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25 million program to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the federal government. Qualifying tipsters would receive a 1% commission. The announcement was made alongside independent journalist Nick Shirley.

Separately, the Department of Homeland Security launched a nationwide ICE operation targeting illegal immigrants accused of fraudulently obtaining benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, resulting in multiple arrests, Fox News reported. Supporters of the administration's approach say it protects taxpayer money and rewards citizens who expose abuse. Critics of such efforts have often raised concerns about whether enforcement is targeted fairly and about the incentives created by commission-based tips, though the available coverage did not detail specific objections to this program.

At the same event, Trump said it was too early to think about endorsing a successor. Vance said he believes Trump would endorse him for 2028 but that they have not discussed a run. The program comes with midterm elections two weeks away and with fraud a prominent theme for the administration. Details on how the commission will be calculated and paid have yet to be fully spelled out in the reporting provided.

stories.headline: Update: Ramaswamy Campaign Spends $4 Million on Ad Featuring Rival Amy Acton's Estranged Mother
stories.summary:
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor is putting $4 million behind an ad in which Democrat Amy Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, calls her daughter a "liar" and urges voters to reject her. Axios reported the buy, saying the campaign is doubling down despite bipartisan backlash. Ramaswamy confirmed to reporters Tuesday that "it is an ad from our campaign."

In the spot, Arthur disputes Acton's account of her upbringing and her claims of childhood abuse. Acton has said her mother sided with her stepfather after he sexually assaulted her at age 12. Acton's brother called the ad a "despicable low" and said their stepfather abused Acton as a child. Acton accused Ramaswamy of a "lifelong pattern" of personal attacks.

Criticism has crossed party lines. Meghan McCain called it a "dastardly ad," and Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown demanded that Republican Sen. Jon Husted condemn it. Ramaswamy's campaign is gambling that the message will resonate with voters in a race NBC News describes as tightening in its final two weeks. Ramaswamy's allies have defended the ad as a legitimate challenge to Acton's personal narrative, while opponents call it exploitation of a family trauma.
